anchor: an unlucky date
note: The Chinese says plainly that the day was unlucky in Western eyes (在西方人眼里). Thirteen carries no such charge in Chinese, where the ominous number is four, 四 sì, being a near-homophone of 死 sǐ, to die. The author opens by borrowing a foreign superstition to cast a shadow, a small piece of exoticism that reads as portentous in Chinese and merely flat in English.

anchor: flying the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth
note: 青天白日满地红, the full descriptive name of the Nationalist flag: a white twelve-rayed sun on a blue canton, on a red field. The canton was designed by Lu Haodong in 1895; Sun Yat-sen added the red field in 1906. The Guangzhou government adopted it in May 1921, but it did not become the official national flag of the Republic until December 1928 — over a year after this scene. In October 1927 it was still the flag of one faction among several, and the Five-Colored Flag remained the Republic's nominal standard. So a warship flying it on the Yangtze is making a claim, not stating a fact: this vessel belongs to Chiang's Nanjing regime. Chinese names the flag by describing it, which English cannot do without sounding like a heraldic label.

anchor: She had steamed down from Wuhu
note: Wuhu, a treaty port on the Yangtze in southern Anhui and Chen Diaoyuan's provincial base. The run downriver to Pukou is roughly 100 km.

anchor: Chen Diaoyuan, Superintendent of Military Affairs for Anhui Province
note: Chen Diaoyuan (陈调元, born 1886 in Xinxian, Hebei) was a Beiyang officer who served a succession of masters — the Zhili clique, then the Fengtian army after surrendering Xuzhou without a fight, then Sun Chuanfang — before secretly opening negotiations with the Northern Expedition and going over to the Nationalists in early 1927 with more than twenty thousand men. Chiang made him commander of the new 37th Army and handed him Anhui. The book's contempt for him as a professional turncoat is the standard verdict, though sources vary on the details of his career. 军务督办, Superintendent of Military Affairs, is a Beiyang-era provincial military governorship held separately from civil office; the author stacks Chen's titles deliberately, to show a man accumulating everything at once.

anchor: Son of a bitch. So the Chen bastard really came.
note: 他妈的 and 王八蛋 in the original. The first is the standard all-purpose Chinese obscenity, literally "his mother's," with the object of the verb left unsaid. The second is literally "turtle's egg," an old and genuinely cutting insult implying the man's mother was unfaithful and his paternity unknown. English has no equivalent that keeps the specific slur about parentage without sounding archaic, so "bastard" carries it at the cost of the animal.

anchor: Under a tree near the wharf
note: The tree is uncertain. The scan degrades exactly here and the character recognition returns 黄栏机 and 黄柳树 on successive passes, neither of which is a word. The most likely reading is 黄桷树 (also written 黄葛树), Ficus virens, a large fig common in southwest China — which is what produced "banyan" in an earlier draft of this translation. But that species is unusual in Nanjing, and 黄杨 (boxwood) and other 木-radical tree names are equally consistent with the damaged glyph. I have left the tree unnamed in the English rather than assert a species I cannot read. Anyone with access to a clean copy of the second edition could settle it in a moment.

anchor: a man got up as a seller of Jinling dates
note: 金陵, Jinling, is the classical literary name for Nanjing, still used for local products and in elevated prose. So the disguise is specifically that of a Nanjing street hawker, not a generic peddler.

anchor: every man with a Mauser in his fist
note: 盒子枪, literally "box gun": the Mauser C96 "broomhandle," so called in Chinese for the wooden holster that doubled as a shoulder stock. Also known as 驳壳枪 or 盒子炮. It was the defining sidearm of the Republican era, carried by warlord guards, gangsters and Communist commanders alike, and its appearance in a scene is a period marker as precise as a Thompson gun in an American one.

anchor: the head of the Hatchet Gang, Wang Yaqiao
note: 斧头帮. Most English writing renders this "Axe Gang," but 斧头 is a hand axe or hatchet, and the organisation took its name from the small axes that Anhui dockworkers carried for cutting cargo ropes — Wang is said to have had a hundred of them forged overnight during a labour dispute around 1921. I have used "Hatchet Gang" both because it is the more accurate object and because "Axe Gang" now drags in associations from Stephen Chow's Kung Fu Hustle that would badly mislead a reader here. The gang grew out of Anhui native-place and labour associations in Shanghai and became a political assassination outfit rather than a conventional criminal syndicate.

anchor: This was the Hefei notable they called the Ninth Master
note: 九爷, "Ninth Master." 爷 is a term of deference for a senior man in this world, closer to "boss" or "the old man" than to any English word for master. The nine comes from Wang's courtesy name 九光, Jiuguang, which he uses of himself later in this section. English cannot show that the honorific and the name are the same nine, so the connection that is obvious on the page in Chinese has to be pointed at here instead.

anchor: a pot of aged nü'erhong
note: 女儿红, "daughter's red," a Shaoxing yellow rice wine traditionally buried in the ground when a daughter is born and dug up for her wedding feast. It is the wine of celebrations and long patience. The author has Wang drinking it while he waits to kill a man, which is either a fine touch or an accident of stock vocabulary; the register of the detail is entirely lost if you simply call it rice wine.

anchor: commander of the 37th Army of the National Revolutionary Army and commander-in-chief of the Northern Route Army besides
note: The character recognition read 莱 here, which is meaningless; the scan clearly shows 兼, "concurrently holding," a bureaucratic term that does real work in this sentence by piling one command on top of another. The 37th Army was the formation created for Chen on his defection.

anchor: Bo Wenwei, commander of the 33rd Army
note: 柏文蔚 (1876–1947), an Anhui revolutionary of the older generation: Tongmenghui member, military governor of Anhui after the 1911 revolution, and a participant in the Second Revolution against Yuan Shikai. His real connection to Wang Yaqiao is documented — Bo was elected chairman of the Anhui Labour Union in Shanghai while Wang actually ran it — which is the factual seed the book grows into this teacher-and-disciple relationship. Note the arithmetic of the scene: the 33rd Army for the old revolutionary, the 37th for the man who changed sides last year.

anchor: He plays the tiger's jackal
note: 为虎作伥. A 伥 chāng is the ghost of a person eaten by a tiger, condemned to serve the beast by luring fresh victims into its path. The idiom therefore means far more than "accomplice": it carries the idea of a soul already devoured, doing the devourer's work, unable to stop. No English phrase reaches it. "Jackal" gets the servility and loses the horror.

anchor: It's the flesh and marrow of the people of Anhui
note: 民脂民膏, "the people's fat and the people's grease." A classical formula for wealth squeezed out of the governed, best known from the admonition carved on stone before magistrates' halls under the Song, warning officials that their salaries were paid in exactly this substance. To a Chinese reader the phrase arrives with the weight of a thousand years of official moralising behind it; in English it can only sound like vivid metaphor.

anchor: several warships were bearing toward him in an A formation
note: 呈A字形 — the original really does use the Latin letter A. Chinese more often describes such shapes with a character, as in 人字形 for a chevron. The Roman letter is a small modernism, and slightly incongruous in a 1927 scene.

anchor: aboard the *Dongzheng*
note: 东征号, the Eastern Expedition, named for the 1925 campaigns in Guangdong that made Chiang's military reputation.

anchor: greeted Chiang first with a student's formal bow
note: 执学生大礼, "performed the full ritual of a student." Chen is claiming the relation of disciple to teacher, the hierarchy that bound the Whampoa Military Academy officers to Chiang — despite having no Whampoa background whatever. That is precisely why it works. The gesture converts a defeated rival into a junior member of Chiang's own house, and Chiang, who valued that hierarchy above nearly everything, takes the offer.

anchor: British mortars and Krupp field guns
note: I flagged this in an earlier pass as the sort of colourful detail the genre invents, and I was wrong: independent accounts of Chen Diaoyuan's defection also report that he presented Chiang with a consignment of first-rate weapons to demonstrate his sincerity. The book's version is embroidered but not fabricated. Krupp guns were the standard German field artillery of the period and widely held by Chinese armies.

anchor: ranged in neat order on the deck
note: The Chinese reads 二门炮, literally "two guns" — 门 being the measure word for artillery pieces. That sits badly against the preceding sentence, which says the deck was loaded with artillery of every kind. Either the author means the two types just named, which is how I have translated it, or the figure is simply careless. I have checked the characters twice against the scan at magnification; the text does read 二.

anchor: I heard you were a Westernized officer
note: 洋军官. 洋 means foreign in the specific sense of Western, and carries a faint edge — 洋 things are modern, impressive and not quite ours. Chiang's compliment is therefore backhanded and double-edged: I had heard you were too foreign, and I find you know your manners after all. The sting and the flattery are the same sentence.

anchor: the governance of Anhui belongs to no one but you
note: 非君莫属, a set literary phrase of high courtesy meaning roughly "it could fall to no one but you, sir." Chiang shifts register upward at the exact moment he hands over a province.

anchor: became the piece Chiang Kai-shek planted on the Anhui board
note: 棋子, a playing piece in weiqi or Chinese chess. The metaphor is a commonplace of Chinese political writing and unremarkable in the original; "pawn" would be too contemptuous and too specifically Western, since weiqi has no ranked pieces. The reading of these characters is somewhat uncertain in the scan, but the sense is not in doubt.

anchor: Wang Yaqiao might have been Mount Tai
note: 安若泰山, "as settled as Mount Tai." Taishan, the eastern sacred peak in Shandong, is the standard Chinese figure for absolute immovability, the way a rock is in English but with the added weight of imperial pilgrimage and state ritual. It recurs constantly in fixed phrases.

anchor: what medicine his chief was selling from that gourd of his
note: 葫芦里卖的什么药, an everyday idiom for unreadable intentions. The image is an itinerant medicine seller whose wares are hidden inside an opaque dried gourd, so no one can tell what he is peddling until it is bought. I have kept it literal rather than flattening it to "what he was up to," because the gourd is the whole flavour of the line.

anchor: I, Wang Jiuguang, deal squarely with the world
note: 王九光. Wang naming himself in full mid-oath is a register marker with no English equivalent — it is the verbal equivalent of standing up. It also settles a question the translation had to resolve: 九光 is Wang Yaqiao's own courtesy name, so the speech earlier in this section beginning "Jiuguang, my friend" is Bo Wenwei addressing Wang, not Wang addressing a third party. An earlier draft of this translation left that ambiguous.

anchor: on his way to call on Chiang Kai-shek
note: The tactical reasoning is worth pausing on, because it is the book's thesis in miniature. Wang is not calling off the killing; he is relocating it, so that Chen's death reads as a message addressed to Chiang. This is assassination as political communication, which is what distinguished Wang Yaqiao from the Green Gang bosses he competed with. He would go on to attempt Chiang himself at Lushan in 1931 and to organise the killing that wounded Wang Jingwei in 1935.

anchor: that political hoodlum, Chiang the Baldhead
note: 蒋光头, "Chiang Bald-head," a standard derisive epithet of the period referring to Chiang's shaven scalp. It sounds cruder in Chinese than "the Baldhead" does in English, closer to a schoolyard name, and its constant use by his enemies was a small ongoing insult to a man extremely conscious of dignity.

anchor: the show they had been preparing since dawn had closed before the curtain ever rose
note: 一场好戏，还没开场就已经谢幕了 — literally "a fine opera that took its curtain call before the curtain ever went up." 开场 and 谢幕 are both theatre terms. Worth flagging because I nearly lost this line: the scan cut off mid-sentence at the foot of the page and an earlier draft closed the section with an invented sentence of my own. The author's ending is better than the one I made up, which is a useful lesson about where translation errors come from.

anchor: Wang Yaqiao had drained a bowl of blood-wine
note: 血酒. Wine mixed with blood, drunk to seal an oath of brotherhood or a vow. The gesture places Wang's promise to Bo Wenwei in the register of sworn kinship rather than mere agreement.

anchor: Zhang Wensheng, a former military governor of Anhui
note: 张文生, a Beiyang general who held Anhui in the early 1920s under the Zhili clique. The book's claim that Wang Yaqiao's agitation helped drive him from office is put in his own mouth here and I have not verified it independently. 寓公, the word behind "comfortable retirement," is a specific Republican type: an ex-official living privately, often in a treaty port or the capital, on the proceeds of office.

anchor: Once bitten by a snake, you shy at a well-rope for ten years
note: 一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳 — the coiled rope at a well's edge looks enough like a snake to make a bitten man flinch. One of the most common of all Chinese proverbs, and given here in its standard form; the scan is damaged at exactly this phrase and the number of years is not fully legible.

anchor: Who's eaten a leopard's gall
note: 吃了豹子胆, "eaten a leopard's gall": in traditional physiology the gall bladder is the seat of daring — 胆 appears in nearly every Chinese word for courage — so to have eaten a leopard's is to have swallowed courage beyond your station. English keeps the organ ("gall") but has lost the anatomy behind it.

anchor: betraying Wu Peifu and Cao Kun
note: Wu Peifu and Cao Kun were the leading figures of the Zhili clique, the Beiyang faction Chen Diaoyuan originally served. Cao Kun had bought the presidency of the Republic outright in 1923, one thousand silver dollars per parliamentary vote — worth knowing when the book's characters talk about corruption as though it began with Chen.

anchor: a pauper magnate second only to Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng
note: 穷大亨, "poor tycoon," a deliberate oxymoron: Wang commanded gang power on the scale of the great racketeers while holding, and distributing, comparatively little money. Huang Jinrong — simultaneously the top Chinese detective in the French Concession police and a crime boss — and Du Yuesheng, master of the opium trade and later Chiang's indispensable ally, were the two summits of the Green Gang. Contemporary accounts agree that these two genuinely preferred to avoid the Hatchet Gang rather than fight it, which for Shanghai in the 1920s is a remarkable fact.

anchor: the Shanghai militarist Sun Wancheng
note: The episode is broadly consistent with the record — Wang Yaqiao did raise a force at Hefei around the 1911 revolution and was driven out — but I cannot attest this commander's name in English-language scholarship, and the scan is rough here; the romanization is provisional.

anchor: Wang Yaqiao's Maicheng days
note: 走麦城, "walking to Maicheng." Maicheng is where Guan Yu — the greatest hero of the Three Kingdoms, later deified as the god of war — made his last retreat and was captured and executed. To "walk to Maicheng" is the proverbial figure for a great man's season of defeat. Zhang Wensheng is being literate and slightly mocking at once.

anchor: He attached himself to Jiang Kanghu
note: 江亢虎 (1883–1954), founder of the Chinese Socialist Party in 1911, the first party in China to carry the name. This detail is genuine history: Wang Yaqiao really did join the party and head its Anhui branch, and Yuan Shikai really did suppress it as he moved toward his imperial restoration. Jiang Kanghu's own road ended badly — he served in Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government during the Japanese occupation and died in a Communist prison.

anchor: Under Purple Mountain the autumn rain
note: 紫金山, Purple-Gold Mountain, the peak that overhangs Nanjing on the east. Its slopes hold the Ming founder's tomb and, from 1929, Sun Yat-sen's mausoleum — which gives the mountain's shadow over this chapter a certain irony the author may or may not intend, given whose testament Wang believes he is enforcing.

anchor: near the Gate of China
note: 中华门, the immense southern gate of the Nanjing city wall, the largest such gate-fortress in China; the surrounding wards were dense, poor, and easy to disappear into.

anchor: the old loach
note: 老泥鳅. The loach is a mudfish, impossible to hold: it slips through the fingers and buries itself in the bottom. Applied to a man it means a slippery survivor — and the sentence extends the same image, 沉沙卧底, "sunk into the sand to lie on the bottom." The metaphor is continuous in the Chinese in a way English can only gesture at.

anchor: Why hasn't he gone to the Confucius Temple
note: The Confucius Temple quarter (夫子庙) on the Qinhuai River was Nanjing's pleasure district — theatres, teahouses, sing-song houses. Wang's question is not about the sage; it means "why isn't he out among the singing girls?" The reply — that the women are brought to him by the carload — answers it in kind.

anchor: his Hatchet Gang lieutenant Kan Peilin
note: The scan is damaged at this name. The surname-glyph as scanned is not a surname at all; 阚 (Kan), a genuine and reasonably common Anhui surname of similar shape, is my best reading, and I have not found the man in outside sources. Treat the romanization as provisional.

anchor: ally with Russia, ally with the Communists, assist the peasants and workers
note: 联俄、联共、扶助农工, the "Three Great Policies" of Sun Yat-sen's last years, the basis of the first United Front with the Communist Party. Whether they represented Sun's true final position or a Soviet-brokered expedient became, after his death in March 1925, the central scriptural dispute of Chinese politics; Chiang's April 1927 purge of the Communists in Shanghai — six months before this scene — was its bloodiest answer. The author has Wang stake his whole vendetta on the orthodox-disciple reading.

anchor: his eye can't take a grain of sand
note: 眼里揉不进沙子, said of a man who cannot let the smallest offence pass. Bo's whole speech runs on set phrases — the next is 小巫见大巫, "the small shaman meeting the great one," rendered here as the small ghost calling on the great one — and the effect in Chinese is of an old man reaching for proverbs because plain words won't carry his alarm.

anchor: I'm a bare-stick proletarian
note: 光棍 — literally "bare stick" or "bare stalk" — means an unattached man: no wife, no property, no ties, and therefore nothing that can be held hostage. Wang's boast is precise: Chiang's forms of leverage need something to grip. The same word appeared earlier where Zhang Wensheng says Wang "stood up a made man" in Shanghai (立起了光棍儿), where it carries its other shading: an established tough, a man of the rivers-and-lakes world.

anchor: a chicken's gut for grievances
note: 小肚鸡肠, "small belly, chicken intestines": no room inside for anything to pass through, hence petty and unforgiving. The judgment of Chiang as a man who never forgot a slight is one point on which his admirers and his enemies broadly agreed.

anchor: the drunkard's interest is not in the wine
note: 醉翁之意不在酒 — from Ouyang Xiu's "Record of the Old Drunkard's Pavilion" (1046), where the writer says his pleasure is not really in the wine but in the mountains and streams. A thousand years of use have worn it into the standard way of saying "my stated purpose is not my real one." That a gang boss reaches for an eleventh-century essayist mid-conspiracy is entirely natural in Chinese and untranslatably strange in English.

anchor: killing the chicken for the monkey to see
note: 杀鸡给猴看: the trainer kills a chicken in front of the monkey, and the monkey — too valuable to harm directly — draws the conclusion. This is the chapter's thesis stated as barnyard proverb: Chen is the chicken; Chiang is the monkey.

anchor: the Jing Ke of our history
note: 荆轲, the most famous assassin in Chinese history, sent in 227 BC against the future First Emperor with a dagger rolled in a map. He failed and was cut down; the verse he sang at the river crossing — the wind sighs, the Yi water is cold; the hero once gone will not return — has stood ever since for the man who accepts death in the act of tyrannicide. Bo Wenwei's blessing is double-edged in a way English can't compress: Jing Ke is glorious, and Jing Ke did not come back. The section heading of the book's thirteenth chapter quotes the same verse, so the author is planting the figure early.

anchor: squatting here like frogs at the bottom of a well
note: The well-frog (井底之蛙), from Zhuangzi: the frog at the bottom of a well believes its circle of sky is the whole of it. Standard shorthand for complacent ignorance; Wang applies it to his own men, which is how the author lets him be furious and self-critical in one breath.

anchor: Zhang Qiubai — Commissioner of Construction
note: 张秋白. A real figure of this name existed in Nationalist politics; whether the historical man's career matches the office and the fate given here I have not been able to establish, and this book is not the sort of source that settles such questions. The nickname the text gives him — 张扒皮, "Zhang the Flayer," rendered below as the people of Anhui called him — is the traditional epithet for a rapacious official or landlord, the man who skins those under him.

anchor: the Ming emperor's tomb near at hand
note: 明孝陵, the Xiaoling mausoleum of the founding Ming emperor Zhu Yuanzhang, on the southern slope of Purple Mountain. Plum Blossom Hill (梅花山), where the killers lie up, is the tomb's forecourt hill — it holds the burial mound of Sun Quan, the third-century king of Wu. The author has chosen his ground: an ambush laid among six centuries of imperial dead.

anchor: war never tires of deception
note: 兵不厌诈, the proverbial condensation of Sun Tzu; and 虚而实之，实而虚之 — "empty where solid, solid where empty" — in the next breath is the Art of War's doctrine of feints, quoted by a gunman to justify storming a dinner party. Popular fiction likes its toughs classically read.

anchor: a high spirit screen carved with two characters — Great Felicity
note: The 影壁 or spirit screen is the free-standing wall just inside or before a traditional gate, blocking sight-lines (and, in folklore, straight-flying spirits). 鸿禧, "vast felicity," is a standard auspicious inscription; the author sets the word FELICITY over the door of the house where the wrong man is about to be shot, and I decline to believe that is an accident.

anchor: four Eight Immortals tables in a row
note: 八仙桌, the square table seating two a side, eight in all, named for the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend. The standard furniture of any formal Chinese dinner; kept literal here for its flavor.

anchor: An injustice has its author; a debt has its owner
note: 冤有头，债有主 — every wrong has a head, every debt a master: the classic announcement of Chinese underworld etiquette, spoken when armed men enter a room full of bystanders. It promises precision — we are here for one man — and it makes what actually happens at this banquet, three bullets into a man merely for delivering bad news, a self-indictment the author leaves entirely unremarked.

anchor: the familiar long horse-face
note: 马型长脸. Worth noting that the author has already shown us this face through Wang Yaqiao's binoculars in section 1, looking like "a man of letters." The horse-faced description here is the killers' file-photograph memory of the same man — the book is casual about focalization, and details shift with the describer.
